Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Expectation2: Take and record vital signs like temperature, pulse, and blood pressure
Situation2: A patient is recovering from a recent procedure and has slightly elevated vital signs.
Story: My phone buzzed in my pocket just as I was about to check Mr. Lee’s blood pressure. I glanced at the screen—my best friend, Sam. I hesitated, but answered quietly, “Hey, Sam, what’s up?” His voice trembled, “Can you talk? I really need you right now. Jess and I had a huge fight.” I could hear the pain in his words, and my instinct was to listen, to be there for him like I always promised. But as I looked at Mr. Lee, pale and anxious after his surgery, I remembered the nurse’s instructions: monitor his vitals every fifteen minutes, report any changes immediately. His last reading was a bit high. My heart pounded as I tried to split my attention, but I knew I couldn’t give either of them what they needed at the same time. Sam’s voice cracked, “Are you there?” I squeezed the blood pressure cuff, feeling torn, guilt rising in my chest. I wanted to be the friend Sam could count on, but I was also responsible for Mr. Lee’s care. The weight of both expectations pressed down on me, and I stood frozen, caught between two worlds, unsure which to choose.
